interest: This document provides valuable insight into the formal diplomatic protocols and court ceremonial traditions of imperial Japan, highlighting the continued reliance on Meiji-era regulations—originally published in French as the international diplomatic lingua franca—well into the 1930s. It also illustrates routine interwar State Department efforts to assemble comparative data on foreign ceremonial and protocol practices, while revealing the mundane archival constraints embassies encountered when host foreign ministries exhausted stocks of official protocol manuals.
overview: This file consists of a two-page diplomatic despatch (No. 653) dated January 24, 1934, from United States Ambassador to Japan Joseph C. Grew to the Secretary of State in Washington. Writing in response to a Department of State circular instruction regarding the procurement of data relating to ceremonial, Grew identifies the primary Japanese publications on protocol: the 1923 'Protocole des Ambassadeurs' and a 1905 guide approved by the Emperor concerning the introduction and presentation of foreign ambassadors extraordinary and plenipotentiary at the Imperial Court. Grew notes that the Japanese Foreign Office was unable to furnish copies because the print editions were exhausted, and expresses hope that copies sent upon their original publication were still on file in Washington.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports to the Secretary of State on the availability of Japanese official publications regarding diplomatic protocol and imperial court etiquette.
subfiles.summary: In response to the Department of State's circular instruction of November 6, 1933, regarding the procurement of ceremonial data, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on existing protocol publications in Japan. He identifies two official publications: the 1923 'Protocole des Ambassadeurs' and the 1905 'Étiquette Approuvée Par Sa Majesté L'Empereur Pour L'Introduction et la Présentation d'un Ambassadeur Extraordinaire et Plénipotentiaire Étranger à la Cour Impériale du Japon.' Grew explains that the Japanese Foreign Office is unable to provide additional copies because the editions are out of print, noting his hope that previously transmitted copies remain on file in the Department.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 653 from Joseph C. Grew to Secretary of State on Procurement of Data Relating to Ceremonial
